lead: A rigid body in general plane motion slides and turns at the same time. Every point stays in a plane parallel to a fixed plane. Choose any point A on the body as a base; the body translates with A and rotates about A. This splitting turns a hard motion into two simple ones. You meet it in a rolling wheel, a connecting rod in an engine, and a door swinging as its hinge moves. The same idea gives the velocity and acceleration of every point.
prereq: You need: translation and fixed-axis rotation from 6.1, and relative motion of particles from Unit 5, Kinematics and Kinetics of Particles.

sections.h3: Splitting the motion into two parts

blocks.text: Plane motion means every point of the body stays in a plane parallel to one fixed plane. Draw the body in that plane and choose a base point A. The body reaches its new position by translating every point with A, then rotating the body about A. Translation gives every point the velocity v_A. Rotation about A gives point B the extra velocity ω × r_{B/A}, where ω is the angular velocity of the body in rad/s and r_{B/A} is the position vector from A to B in metres. In plane motion ω is perpendicular to the plane, so the extra velocity has magnitude ω r_{B/A} and points perpendicular to AB.

blocks.where: v_B and v_A are the velocities of points B and A (m/s); ω is the body's angular velocity (rad/s); r_{B/A} is the vector from A to B (m); × is the vector cross product. The relative term is perpendicular to AB.

blocks.text: Differentiate the velocity equation. The base accelerates with a_A. Rotation about A adds a tangential part and a centripetal part. The angular acceleration α (rad/s²) gives the tangential term α × r_{B/A}, of magnitude α r_{B/A}, perpendicular to AB. The spin gives the centripetal term −ω² r_{B/A}, of magnitude ω² r_{B/A}, pointing from B to A. So a_B = a_A + α × r_{B/A} − ω² r_{B/A}. The minus sign matters: the centripetal term points toward the base A, not away from it. Some syllabi call these the absolute and relative velocity and acceleration equations.
a_B = a_A + α × r_{B/A} − ω² r_{B/A}
blocks.where: a_B, a_A are accelerations (m/s²); α is angular acceleration (rad/s²); ω is angular velocity (rad/s); r_{B/A} is the vector from A to B (m). The α × r term is tangential; the −ω² r term points from B to A.

blocks.text: A wheel of radius R rolls without slipping on a fixed road. Let G be its centre and C the contact point. No slipping means the contact point has zero velocity at that instant: v_C = 0. Put C as the base in v_G = v_C + ω × r_{G/C}; this gives v_G = ωR. Differentiating gives a_G = αR for the centre on a straight road. The top point T has v_T = v_G + ωR = 2v_G because its rotation velocity and the centre velocity point the same way. The contact point has v_C = 0, so it is the instantaneous centre for that instant; see 6.4.

items: Rolling without slipping: v_G = ωR, a_G = αR, v_C = 0.
Contact point is the instantaneous centre for that instant.

figure.caption: Translation of base point A and rotation about A combine to give point B's velocity and acceleration. Notice the two equations in the last row.

spec.title: General plane motion
spec.aria: Plane motion combines translation of a base point with rotation about that point to give the velocity and acceleration equations.

examples.question: A wheel of radius 0.40 m rolls without slipping on a horizontal road. Its centre moves at 3.0 m/s. Find (a) the angular velocity of the wheel, (b) the speed of the top point, and (c) the speed of the contact point.
steps: Data: R = 0.40 m, v_G = 3.0 m/s. Rolling without slipping means the contact point C has v_C = 0.
Angular velocity: v_G = ω R, so ω = v_G / R = 3.0 / 0.40 = 7.5 rad/s.
Contact point: v_C = v_G − ω R = 3.0 − 3.0 = 0 m/s.
examples.answer: ω = 7.5 rad/s, top point speed = 6.0 m/s, contact point speed = 0 m/s.
examples.check:
R = 0.40
vG = 3.0
omega = vG / R
v_top = vG + omega * R
v_contact = vG - omega * R
print(omega)
print(v_top)
print(v_contact)

traps: Adding ωR to every point in the same direction. On a rolling wheel the top point gets +ωR, the bottom point gets −ωR, and the contact point has zero velocity.
Dropping the centripetal term −ω² r in acceleration. A point on a rotating body always has ω² r toward the centre even when α = 0.
Using r_{B/A} in the wrong direction. r_{B/A} points from A to B; reversing it reverses the relative velocity and tangential acceleration.
Treating the instantaneous centre as a fixed point. It moves from instant to instant; only for that instant is the body in pure rotation about it.
Mixing rad/s with rev/min. Convert revolutions per minute to rad/s by multiplying by 2π/60 before using v = ωr.

quiz.q: State the velocity equation for points A and B on a rigid body in plane motion, defining each symbol.
quiz.a: v_B = v_A + ω × r_{B/A}; v_A and v_B are velocities (m/s), ω is angular velocity (rad/s), r_{B/A} is the vector from A to B (m).

quiz.q: Why is the relative velocity ω × r_{B/A} perpendicular to AB?
quiz.a: ω is perpendicular to the plane; the cross product of a perpendicular vector with a vector in the plane lies in the plane and perpendicular to r_{B/A}. Rotation moves B along the tangent to its circular path about A.

quiz.q: A link AB of length 0.50 m rotates about fixed point A with ω = 4 rad/s and α = 0. Find the speed of B and the magnitude of its acceleration.
quiz.a: v_B = ω r = 4 × 0.50 = 2.0 m/s. a_B = ω² r = 4² × 0.50 = 8.0 m/s², directed from B to A. α = 0 gives no tangential term.

quiz.q: A wheel of radius 0.25 m rolls without slipping with centre speed 2.0 m/s and centre acceleration 1.5 m/s². Find ω, α, and the acceleration magnitude of the top point.
quiz.a: ω = v_G/R = 2.0/0.25 = 8 rad/s. α = a_G/R = 1.5/0.25 = 6 rad/s². At the top, tangential parts add: 1.5 + 6×0.25 = 3.0 m/s² horizontal; centripetal part is ω²R = 64×0.25 = 16 m/s² downward. Magnitude = √(3.0² + 16²) = 16.3 m/s².

quiz.q: A ladder slides with its foot moving horizontally and its top moving vertically. Describe how to locate the instantaneous centre using the velocity directions.
quiz.a: Draw a perpendicular to the foot velocity at the foot; it is vertical. Draw a perpendicular to the top velocity at the top; it is horizontal. Their intersection is the instantaneous centre. It is generally not the midpoint; the midpoint is the centre only in special positions.

quiz.q: Why can the contact point of a rolling wheel be used as the instantaneous centre even though it is momentarily at rest?
quiz.a: At that instant its velocity is zero, so the wheel's motion is a pure rotation about that point. The centre and top velocities follow from v = ωr about the contact point.

quiz.q: Write the acceleration equation and state the direction of the −ω² r_{B/A} term.
quiz.a: a_B = a_A + α × r_{B/A} − ω² r_{B/A}. The −ω² r_{B/A} term points from B to A, toward the base point.

beyond: Not for the exam. General plane motion is the base for robot-arm kinematics, vehicle dynamics, and multibody simulation. Search 'relative velocity method rigid body', 'rolling constraint', and 'instantaneous centre'. In CAD and game engines, the same equations update every rigid part each frame.
